page: The Amazon Web Services m2.2xlarge is an earlier-generation instance provisioned on the Xen hypervisor, configured with 4 dedicated physical cores on an Intel Xeon E5-2665 processor clocked at 2.4 GHz. It features an x86_64 architecture with 20 MB of L3 cache, 34.0 GB of system memory delivering 8.55 GB per core, and an integrated 850 GB local hard disk drive (HDD). Network connectivity provides a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps, and the configuration contains zero GPU accelerators.

Benchmark results reflect the legacy nature of the underlying hardware platform. In synthetic compute evaluations, the instance scores 666.0 in single-core Geekbench and 1433.0 in multi-core tests, accompanied by a PassMark CPU score of 2609.62, placing CPU throughput in the lower percentiles. The absence of modern instruction extensions such as AVX and hardware-accelerated AES impacts cryptographic and vector performance, with PassMark encryption registering 549.71. Conversely, the memory subsystem demonstrates stable throughput, achieving an average tier PassMark memory score of 2020.29 and 26.32 GB/sec uncached read bandwidth.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the resource profile is heavily weighted toward high RAM density and local mechanical storage rather than raw computational throughput. The trade-off lies in substantial memory availability paired with slower rotational disk access and diminished CPU throughput relative to contemporary platforms. Workload suitability centers on legacy systems, memory-demanding background tasks, staging environments, and batch operations that require large memory allocations without demanding intensive compute power or fast disk I/O.
description: The Amazon Web Services m2.2xlarge is a legacy instance powered by a 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2665 processor, providing 4 dedicated vCPUs alongside 34.0 GB of memory and an 850 GB local HDD. Deployed on the Xen hypervisor with an x86_64 architecture, it offers a baseline network speed of 1 Gbps without hardware GPU acceleration. Benchmark evaluations place processing capacity in lower tiers, recorded at 666.0 for Geekbench single-core and 1433.0 for multi-core, while PassMark memory achieves an average tier score of 2020.29. The absence of modern cryptographic and vector extensions impacts intensive processing routines. Given the 8.55 GB of RAM per core paired with rotational storage, the instance prioritizes memory capacity over raw computation. It is primarily suitable for memory-heavy legacy workloads, basic caching tiers, and non-intensive background processing that require sizable memory buffers without requiring high CPU instruction throughput.
